summary: Describes interoperability scenarios for using Provider Backbone Bridge functionality in Hierarchical VPLS, with Ethernet or MPLS access, to improve scalability in customer MAC addresses and service instances. It is informational rather than a new protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: Hierarchical VPLS splits a carrier's network into an access tier and a core, but the core still has to learn every customer address. Provider Backbone Bridging hides those addresses inside provider addresses and gives each service a 24-bit identifier. This RFC describes how the two can be mixed, including how an operator can move over gradually.

subtitle: How to mix Provider Backbone Bridging into Hierarchical VPLS without replacing the installed base.

tldr.problem: Hierarchical VPLS scales by splitting the provider network into an access tier and a core, but the core still learns every customer MAC address and still needs a full mesh of pseudowires per service instance, and a QinQ access network runs out of service identifiers at 4094.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes how IEEE 802.1ah Provider Backbone Bridging can be used in the access network. PBB tunnels customer MAC addresses inside provider addresses, so the core only sees provider addresses, and it carries a 24-bit I-SID service identifier that allows up to 16M services per access network.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational RFC describing interoperability scenarios rather than a protocol. It covers two service interfaces for a VPLS provider edge, mixed access networks, and three migration paths that let an operator adopt PBB gradually.

today: RFC 7080 is an Informational RFC published in December 2013. It has not been obsoleted or updated. It remains a description of interoperability scenarios for using Provider Backbone Bridging in H-VPLS rather than a specification of a protocol.

sections.title: Why Bring PBB into VPLS
sections.content:
The scalability of Hierarchical Virtual Private LAN Service with Ethernet access networks, as described in RFC 4762, can be improved by incorporating Provider Backbone Bridge functionality in the VPLS access. Provider Backbone Bridging was standardised as IEEE 802.1ah-2008, an amendment to IEEE 802.1Q, to improve the scalability of MAC addresses and service instances in Provider Ethernet networks.

Two limits make this worth doing. In H-VPLS the learning and forwarding of MAC addresses is based on customer MAC addresses, so the number of MAC addresses each provider edge holds grows with the number of VPLS instances. Separately, a set of pseudowires is maintained per customer service instance, so the number of pseudowires a network-facing provider edge needs is the number of service instances multiplied by the number of provider edges in the full mesh. That is a problem for pseudowire manageability and troubleshooting as the number of service instances grows. In an 802.1ad Ethernet access network there is a third limit: the number of provider VLANs is capped at 4094, and each one represents a service instance, so at most 4094 service instances can be supported.

PBB addresses the first two problems by using MAC tunnelling encapsulation, which shows the provider's own MAC addresses to the provider edge nodes instead of the customers'. It addresses the third with the new 24-bit service identifier, the I-SID, which allows up to 16M services per PBB access network against 4094 for 802.1Q or 802.1ad access. It also separates the service layer from the network layer, because the I-SID identifies the service while the backbone VLAN identifies the broadcast domain, and in 802.1ad access networks those two layers are the same thing.
sections.plainLanguage: The core of a hierarchical VPLS has to remember every customer address and carry a separate wire for every service. PBB hides customer addresses and packs many services onto one wire.

sections.title: The Labels in Play
sections.content:
The RFC defines a set of labels that appear in every scenario it describes.

C-MACs are the customer MAC addresses, the inner addresses of a PBB-encapsulated frame. B-MACs are the backbone MAC addresses, the outer addresses of such a frame. The B-TAG is a field in the 802.1ah encapsulation header that carries the backbone VLAN identifier, in the same format as the 802.1ad S-TAG, and the specific identifier inside it is the B-VID. The I-TAG carries the service instance information, and the 24-bit I-SID inside it defines the service instance that the frame is mapped to.

The devices are named for the part they play. A BEB is a backbone edge bridge at the edge of a provider backbone bridged network and may hold an I-component, a B-component or both. An IB-BEB holds both, bridging in customer space with customer MAC addresses and S-VLAN identifiers in the I-component and in the provider's backbone space with B-MACs and B-TAGs in the B-component. A BCB is a backbone core bridge in the core of the network, bridging on B-TAG information just as an 802.1ad provider bridge bridges on the S-VLAN identifier.

Two administrative boundaries follow from these labels. An I-SID Domain is a boundary under which every PBB edge bridge and VPLS provider edge uses the same I-SID space, so a service instance has the same I-SID everywhere inside it. A B-VLAN Domain is a boundary under which the grouping of I-SIDs into B-VLANs is consistent. Three kinds of service domain result: tightly coupled, where access networks share both domains; loosely coupled, where they share the I-SID domain but keep their own B-VLAN domains; and different, where each access network has its own I-SID domain as well. Correct connectivity across a tightly coupled domain needs only B-VID mapping, a loosely coupled domain needs I-SID to B-VID remapping, and a different domain needs I-SID translation on top of that.
sections.plainLanguage: Two tags travel with every frame: an outer one for the provider's network and an inner one for the service. When two access networks agree on how to number their services, no translation is needed; when they do not, something has to be rewritten on the way through.

sections.title: The Two Service Interfaces
sections.content:
A VPLS provider edge is always part of the IP/MPLS core, and it may optionally take part in the control protocols of the access network. When it connects to a PBB access network it has to support one of two service interfaces.

The Type I interface is a B-tagged service interface with the B-VID as the service delimiter. The provider edge connects to a backbone core bridge, and the handoff is B-tagged PBB-encapsulated frames. Because the B-VID EtherType is the same as the S-VID EtherType, the provider edge treats the frames as 802.1ad frames and stays transparent to PBB encapsulation, so it needs no PBB functionality of its own. This works like a conventional tagged service interface does today, and the edge therefore provides network-level interworking between the PBB access and the MPLS core, because it has no visibility of I-SIDs. Type I supports three modes: port mode, where all traffic on an interface maps to one VPLS instance; VLAN mode, where the traffic of a particular B-VID maps to one VPLS instance; and VLAN bundling mode, where a group or range of B-VIDs maps to one VPLS instance. Its advantage is that many I-SIDs ride one pseudowire, so the core needs far fewer of them, and the core never sees customer MAC addresses. Its disadvantage is heavy replication: because a group of service instances shares one full mesh of pseudowires, an unknown unicast, multicast or broadcast on one service instance floods the whole core, which can be mitigated with flood containment per I-SID.

The Type II interface is an I-tagged service interface with the I-SID as the service delimiter. The provider edge connects to a backbone edge bridge with a B-component, and the edge itself has to implement that B-component so it can process I-SIDs and map a bundle of I-SIDs to a VPLS instance. The service delimiter is now the I-SID, so the edge provides service-level interworking, and the backbone edge bridge removes the B-VLAN tags on the way out. Type II works in loosely coupled and different service domains as well as tightly coupled ones, and it lets an operator trade pseudowire state against multicast containment by setting up a full mesh per I-SID, per group of I-SIDs, or for all I-SIDs at once. With a full mesh per I-SID or per group, replication in the core falls without needing a separate flood containment mechanism, at the cost of more pseudowires.
sections.plainLanguage: Type I hides the service identifier from the provider edge and packs many services onto one wire, but a broadcast then floods everything. Type II lets the edge see the service identifier, so it can group services more carefully and contain the flooding.

sections.title: Mixing PBB Access with Existing Access
sections.content:
Providers will want their existing Provider Bridged Networks, which use 802.1ad QinQ, to interoperate with PBB access networks over H-VPLS. Two cases arise, depending on which provider edge does the interworking.

In the first case the provider edge on the PBB side behaves as it would in a homogeneous PBB network, using the Type II service interface, and the provider edge on the QinQ side has to be modified. It gains IB-BEB functionality, and at its S-tagged service interface the only workable service is a one-to-one mapping of S-VID to I-SID, because a QinQ access network has no I-SID to bundle. Towards the core, that same edge can bundle I-SIDs into a VPLS instance. The assumptions behind this topology are that the customer equipment connects directly to the PBB network through an S-tagged or port-based interface, that the I-SID in the PBB access represents the same customer as the S-VID in the QinQ access, and that the edge joins the local I-SID domain of the core.

In the second case the provider edge on the QinQ side behaves exactly as an existing VPLS provider edge does, and the provider edge on the PBB side has to change. It gains IB-BEB functionality with the I-component facing the core and the B-component facing the PBB access network, and one or more I-SIDs can be grouped into a B-VID inside the PBB access. Here the mapping between I-SID and VPLS instance is one to one, and S-VID bundling on the QinQ side is not viable because it corresponds to nothing in the PBB access. I-SID bundling mode is not supported in this case, because the core behaves exactly as it does today.
sections.plainLanguage: A provider with old QinQ access and new PBB access has to pick one side of the core to do the translating. Either way, the QinQ side can only map one service identifier to one service identifier.

sections.title: PBB with MPLS Access and Migration Paths
sections.content:
For an H-VPLS network with MPLS access, PBB functionality can be embedded either in the user-facing provider edge or in the network-facing one. In current H-VPLS the network-facing edge must learn the customer MAC addresses of every VPLS instance it takes part in, which easily adds up to hundreds of thousands or even millions of addresses. When the user-facing edge performs PBB encapsulation, the network-facing edge only has to learn the MAC addresses of the user-facing edges, which is a significant reduction. Many I-SIDs are then multiplexed inside one bridge domain, so setting up a VPLS instance per backbone VLAN also cuts the number of full-mesh pseudowires. The cost is more replication: customer multicast and broadcast frames are broadcast within the backbone VLAN, which flood containment per I-SID can remedy.

With the PBB function at the user-facing edge, that edge maps each customer service, whether in port, VLAN or VLAN-bundling mode, onto a single I-SID, and then maps a bridge domain onto a VPLS instance. MAC forwarding is based on the B-MAC address space and the service delimiter is the backbone VLAN identifier, so the VPLS network-facing edges never inspect I-SID values. The mirror-image case puts the PBB function at the network-facing edge, where the spoke pseudowire from the user-facing edge is not service multiplexed because there is no PBB functionality on that side.

Operators are unlikely to migrate an installed H-VPLS network overnight, so the RFC sets out three migration scenarios. In the first, only 802.1ad service frames cross the core, as today, and the existing access networks and network-facing edges need no change, though they also gain no MAC or pseudowire scalability. In the second, all frames crossing the core are PBB-encapsulated, which gives the network-facing edges the scalability benefit but requires upgrading every one of them. In the third, the core carries a mix: existing access networks keep exchanging 802.1ad frames while the new PBB networks exchange PBB-encapsulated frames among themselves, and the network-facing edge of the PBB network encapsulates and decapsulates as needed. That last scenario needs the edge to know whether its peer supports PBB, which can come from static configuration or from extending the VPLS control plane. It also needs two point-to-multipoint label-switched paths at the ingress edge, one for peers that support PBB encapsulation and one for those that do not.
sections.plainLanguage: An operator can put PBB in the edge closest to the customer or in the edge facing the core. There are also three ways to move over: keep the old format everywhere, move to the new format everywhere, or run both.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC states that it introduces no additional security aspects beyond those already applicable to VPLS and H-VPLS, and points to RFC 4111 and RFC 4762, where the VPLS and H-VPLS security considerations are already covered.
sections.plainLanguage: This document adds nothing new on security. The VPLS and H-VPLS rules in the earlier RFCs still apply.

viz.caption: THE THREE KINDS OF SERVICE DOMAIN

items.title: Tightly coupled
items.text: Access networks share the I-SID domain and the B-VLAN domain. Connectivity needs B-VID mapping only.

items.title: Loosely coupled
items.text: Access networks share the I-SID domain but keep their own B-VLAN domains. Connectivity needs I-SID to B-VID remapping.

items.title: Different
items.text: Each access network has its own I-SID domain and B-VLAN domain. Connectivity needs I-SID translation and remapping.
